title: Cross-referencing Tasmanian Terrestrial Ecosystems
text:
Overview of this document
This document presents a reproducible computational workflow for the analysis and synthesis of cross-referencing information for Tasmanian terrestrial ecosystems. Cross-referencing aims to elucidate relationships between units of classifications that represent similar types of entities , ?sec-process.
In this document the source classification is the TASVEG dataset (Tasmanian Vegetation Monitoring and Mapping Program 2025; Kitchener and Harris 2013) that includes 159 mapping units, most of them representing ecological vegetation communities (see chapter 2  Source classification: TASVEG). These vegetation communities are aligned with the ecosystem concept of the target classification, the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology (IUCN GET; Keith et al. (2022); see chapter 3  Assess alignment between classifications).
The main body of the document is divided in three parts. The first part includes four chapters dedicated to Data preparation. First, we collect the spatial and ecological information from the source and target classifications 4  Lookup tables for both classifications, and membership tables from five interpreters ?sec-memb-table. Then, we validate and clean the input data, 6  Data validation. Finally, we explore the cleaned dataset with a full membership table including the assessments of the five interpreters in two rounds of interpretation 7  Exploration of the data.
The second part of the document is dedicated to Analysis of the cross-referencing data. We analysed agreement between interpreters and inherent cross-referencing uncertainty for each round of interpretaton 8  Round one, 9  Round two, and compared differences between rounds 10  Between rounds.
The final part of the document presents a synthesis of the cross-referencing information and produces different types of outputs, including, symmary tables and maps.
This online document is a joint output of the ARDC “Ecosystem Indicators Workflows” (EIW) project and the ARC Industry Laureate Fellowship Project “Foundations for leading the nature positive ecosystem conservation agenda”.
You can use the links on the left to navigate through the different sections of this resource.

title: 1  Stepwise cross-referencing process
text:
1.1 Overview of stepwise cross-referencing process
The need to cross-reference different classification systems arises frequently in ecology and conservation applications. The conceptual foundations for cross-referencing classifications are discussed in IUCN (2025).
Here we try to apply consistent methods and standards for cross-referencing in order to make the relationships between units more explicit and enhance the reproducibility of the process. This will enable efficient update when more information becomes available, and minimise divergent or erroneous interpretations of relationships between classifications.
The process of cross-reference involves a source classification and a target classification, where the target classification might have a broader scope than the source. Elements in the source classification can be interpreted as directly related to one or more elements in the target classification. This relationship can be quantified as membership values, where the source element has memberships between 0 and 100% to each element of the target classification.
Membership estimates from multiple interpreters can be combined to produce more robust cross-referencing relationships. Uncertainty due to disagreements between interpreters can be quantified and documented for maximum transparency.
A stepwise diagnostic process ensures that the cross-referencing exercise aligns with four key principles: alignment of classifications, membership based on entity properties, using weight of evidence, and transparent representation of uncertainty (IUCN 2025).
Steps 1 and 2 are essential steps for preparation of the information and decisions that will shape the cross-referencing process. Multiple interpreters might be involved in steps 3 and 4. An additional round of expert elicitation is recommended to try to reduce disagreement.
The process of expert elicitation usually involves:
In step 5 we are interested in compiling membership matrix from multiple interpreters after the elicitation process, linking back to spatial data for visualisation, and documenting and analysing sources of uncertainties.

1.2 Reproducible workflow for cross-referencing
In this document we want to translate the cross-referencing process into a reproducible computation workflow. This computation workflow will take inputs from the interpreters, and describe all steps of data preparation and analysis that lead to specific outputs. The purpose of the workflow is to increase reproducibility of this process that will allow streamlined updates of outputs everytime the input data is updated.
For this process we lean on the R package ecoSynthesis currently under development, as well as on custom scripts and functions, and additional R packages.

title: 2  Source classification: TASVEG
text:
2.1 Components of TASVEG
In this document we are focusing on TASVEG, a comprehensive digital map of Tasmania’s vegetation, including sub-Antarctic Macquarie Island (Tasmanian Vegetation Monitoring and Mapping Program 2013, 2025).
The TASVEG dataset includes ecological and spatial information, and for the purposes of this document we will differentiate between mapping units and vegetation communities.
The majority of the mapping units represent vegetation communities, including coastal heathlands, eucalypt forest and alpine communities. The technical manual (Kitchener and Harris 2013) includes description for each of the 159 mapping units, most of them ecological vegetation communities. The format of these descriptions is consistent, descriptive and cross-referenced with relevant literature and other processes.
TASVEG has several components and we are going to use them in different steps of the process.

title: 3  Assess alignment between classifications
text:
3.1 Eligibility of units
Conceptual alignment is the first principle for cross-referencing classifications. Units in both the source and target classification should be based on similar concepts.
Cross-referencing aims to elucidate relationships between units of classifications that represent similar types of entities. To be cross-referenced to the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology (IUCN GET), it follows that the units of the source classification must be aligned with the ecosystem concept.
Based on the definition agreed upon by Secretariat of the Convention on Biological Diversity (1992), following Tansley (1935) original concept, an ecosystem is:
Qualitatively different kinds of entities should not be compared to the IUCN GET. In some cases partial relationships or conceptual overlaps may arise, and these warrant rigorous evaluation in cross-referencing to determine eligibility. For example land use and land cover classes or types are sometimes used as proxies of structural features of ecosystems, but they lack information on compositional and functional features.
Most units in the TASVEG dataset represent vegetation communities and can be considered eligible for crossreferencing to the IUCN GET.
However, there are three mapping units in the group ‘Other natural environments’ that require more scrutiny: Lichen lithosere (ORO), Sand, mud (OSM), and Water, sea (OAQ).
According to the technical manual (Kitchener and Harris 2013):
The units OAQ and OSM are mapping units combining multiple types of ecosystems

title: 3  Assess alignment between classifications
text:
Lichen lithosere (ORO) is important for undisturbed cryptogamic communities, such as on blockstreams, cliffs, talus and scree slopes and exposed bedrock on mountain tops and ridges.


Sand, mud (OSM) is bare of vegetation, has been used for mapping beaches, sand dune systems, and mobile sand sheets such as those at Waterhouse in north-east Tasmania or at Sandy Cape on the west coast.


Water, sea (OAQ) has been used to designate areas of sea, artificial impoundments such as Lake Gordon, Lake Saint Clair and Lake Pedder, as well as deep water in natural lakes.

5.1 Read membership tables
The objective of this section is to read input data in different formats and create a summary of the relationships in a consistent output format.
Input formats are convenient for data entry, but not optimal for data analysis.
Different experts will work with different types of input formats.
A consistent output format is useful for designing streamlined operations and functions. This format allows better interoperability in data operations.
The output format can be back-transformed to the input formats if required.
We have cross-referencing tables from five interpreters. All files were prepared by MGT in CSV format with a common header but there are two different ways of representing the data.
Most of the files will have a paired-column format with each pair indicating the target unit and membership value (EFG_1, memb_1, etc.).

We use the following code to run through the list of files, read metadata and data, apply the relevant functions according to the shape of the input data, and combine all in a single table.
memb_data <- foreach(j = dir(csv_folder), .combine = bind_rows) %do% {
    metadata <- read_csv(here::here(csv_folder, j),
        col_names = c("name", "value"), n_max = 11, show_col_types = F
    )[, 1:2]
    data <- read_csv(here::here(csv_folder, j), skip = 12, show_col_types = F)

    cat(sprintf("Read %s, interpreter %s\n%s\n", j, metadata[1, 2], metadata[11, 2]))

    if ("EFG_1" %in% colnames(data)) {
        pivot_wide_membership_table(
            xref = data,
            original_names = "VEGCODE",
            target_names = sprintf("EFG_%s", 1:4),
            membership_values = sprintf("memb_%s", 1:4),
            expert_name = metadata[[1, 2]],
            round = if_else(grepl("First", metadata[11, 2]), 1, 2)
        )
    } else {
        pivot_membership_matrix(
            xref = data,
            original_names = "VEGCODE",
            target_names = colnames(data)[-1],
            expert_name = metadata[[1, 2]],
            round = if_else(grepl("First", metadata[11, 2]), 1, 2)
        )
    }
}

11.1 Types of summaries for membership tables
The objective of the synthesis step is to consolidate information from different interpreters on how each source unit is aligned with one or more target units.
We use the membership table as the key data source, and we can aggregate this data in multiple dimensions, but here we are interested in the following:
The shape and form of the summary table for the synthesis step will depend on the combination of the previous decisions. In this document we consider four combinations:

11.1.1 Keep all records


Our setup for this R session is:

library(sf)
library(ecoSynthesis)
library(dplyr)
library(units)
library(ggplot2)
here::i_am("synthesis/index.qmd")
output_dir <- here::here("../results/XREFs")
load(here::here(output_dir, "memb-tables.rda"))

The first option is simply a filtered membership table, where each sources unit will keep all valid records from the selected round:

TASVEG_revised <- TASVEG_clean |>
  filter(round == 2) |>
  group_by(VEGCODE, expert) |>
  mutate(
    total_memb = sum(memb),
    best = memb == max(memb),
    supporting = 1,
    total_interp = 1
  ) |>
  ungroup()

For example, for the source unit AAP:

  filter(VEGCODE == "AAP")

For some applications we want to summmarise across interpreters, and consider all potential target units:

  TASVEG_clean |>
  summarise_membership(keep_all = TRUE, which_round = 2) |>
  mutate(
    best = prop_memb == max(prop_memb),

title: 11  Synthesis overview
text:
11.2 Outputs
The summary of the membership table produces an intermediate output that might still require further steps of transformation.
This is the case for spatial analysis, where we need to merge the membership summary with tables of attributes of the spatial objects in order to get the desired output (a spatial summary or a spatial object for plotting target units or membership values).
In this cases the type of output will constrain the amount of information that can be kept.
We will show two examples in the next two chapters: area summaries in ?sec-areas; and different types of raster maps in Chapter 13.

title: 12  Area summaries
12  Area summaries
text:
12.1.1 Weighted area estimates
For calculations of areas we have to consider that each source unit might be represented by multiple map units, and each map unit might be assigned to more that one target unit.
The calculations in this workflow assume that the relationships between source and target units are the same for all mapping unit within each source unit.
This can be calculated using a left join of both tables with a many to many relationship:

EFG_memb_exp_areas <- TASVEG_areas |> # nolint: object_name_linter.
    left_join(TASVEG_revised, by = "VEGCODE", relationship = "many-to-many") |>
    mutate(EFG = coalesce(EFG, "!XREF"))

Furthermore, we need to decide if we want to adjust the areas to represent uncertainty in the assignment of the relationship. One possible way to adjust the areas is to use the membership value as an estimate of the proportion of the area that can be assigned to the target unit.
Using an example of one target unit (T2.5), we can summarise the data by expert and membership and calculate total areas of the units vs the weighed area estimates:

EFG_memb_exp_areas |>
    filter(EFG == "T2.5") |>
    summarise(
        nr_VEGCODE = n_distinct(VEGCODE),
        mean_memb = mean(memb),
        area_total = set_units(sum(area), "km2"),
        area_weighted = set_units(sum(area * memb), "km2"),
        .by = c(expert, EFG, best)
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(area_total))

Interpreters differ in the nr of source of unit and the mean membership values assigned to those units. Consequently the total and weighted area estimates will be different.
We need to reshape the data if we want to explore this at the level of the source units:

plot_data <- EFG_memb_exp_areas |>
    filter(EFG == "T2.5") |>
    summarise(
        total_area = sum(drop_units(area)),
        .by = all_of(c("expert", "VEGCODE", "memb", "best"))
    ) |>
    mutate(
        sid = reorder(VEGCODE, total_area),
        assigned_area = total_area * memb,
        remaining_area = total_area - assigned_area
    ) |>
    pivot_longer(
        cols = c(assigned_area, remaining_area),
        names_to = "segment", values_to = "height"

    mutate(segment = factor(segment, levels = c("remaining_area", "assigned_area"))) |>
    arrange(sid)

    geom_col(position = "stack") +

    theme_wp3()

13.1 Best candidates from aggregated membership
In order to create spatial outputs from the synthesis of membership values, we need to combine the membership table with the spatial attribute table.
The spatial attribute table attached to the spatial dataset (in Shapefile format) contains one entry per polygon, and hundred of thousands of polygons.
The decisions about how we synthetise the data will constrain the type of data we can export as output. Here we show certain examples.
Here we aggregate the data from the second round of expert elicitation.

title: 14  Glossary
text:
Term
Definition
Examples from this document




Cross-reference (xref) or membership table
A table that summarises assessments of membership of units of one (source) classification to units of another (target) classification.
See ?sec-memb-table and Chapter 15.


Source
The classification being cross-referenced from.
In this document the source classification is TASVEG 5.0, the Tasmanian vegetation mapping. See Chapter 2.


Source unit
One concept or mapping unit of the source classification. Each unit is assessed separately.
In TASVEG the classification units represent vegetation communities, see Chapter 2.


Source unit id / Source id
Unique ids for the units in the source classification.
VEGCODE column in the TASVEG Look-up table (Chapter 4)


Target
The classification being cross-referenced to.
In this document the target classification is the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology, see Chapter 3.


Target unit
One unit of the target classification.
Here we use level 3 of the IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology: Ecosystem Functional Group (EFG), see Chapter 2.


Target unit id / Target id
Unique ids for the units in the target classification.
EFG or efg_id columns. Codes for EFG Codes are realm + biome + group, e.g. T2.6 (terrestrial), F2.2 (freshwater), MT1.3 (marine–terrestrial shoreline), TF1.6 (terrestrial–freshwater wetland), MFT1.3 (marine–freshwater–terrestrial).


Interpreter
The person who made the assessment of memberships.
Here we refer to interpreter or expert interchangeably, see ?sec-memb-table.


Membership
An interpreter’s estimate of the relationship between a source unit and a target unit. Target units have a broader scope, so they can group multiple source units. Memberships are interpreted as fuzzy memberships, such that a source unit might belong to multiple target units. This fuzzy membership is expressed as a continuous value between 0 (excluded from the group) and 1 (unambiguous membership).
See ?sec-memb-table and Chapter 15.


Assigned / not assigned
Each interpreter assigns one or multiple target for each source unit with membership values above 0 (assigned target). The sum of membership values for assigned targets of a single interpreter should sum to 1. Potential targets (for example, those assigned by other interpreters) that are not listed by an interpreter, are considered not assigned and have a membership value of 0.
See ?sec-memb-table.


Not assessed
The interpreter gave no record for the unit at all. This is different from “not assigned” and is never filled with 0.
See ?sec-memb-table.


Record
One interpreter’s membership for one unit and one target. Long format means one record per row.
See ?sec-memb-table.


Profile
An interpreter’s full set of memberships for one unit, across every target that any expert used for that unit.



Matrix table
The data reshaped wide: one row per unit and interpreter, one column per target group.
membership_matrix, see Chapter 15.


Dissimilarity
How different two interpreter’ profiles are for a unit: ½ × the sum of absolute differences, i.e. the share of membership that would have to move to make them identical. 0 = identical, 1 = no shared membership.
dissimilarity


Similarity
1 − dissimilarity. 1 = identical profiles, 0 = no overlap.
similarity


Identical
Two profiles with a dissimilarity of essentially 0 (below 0.001).
share_identical


Expert pair
Two interpreter compared on the same unit. With four interpreter there are six pairs.
expert_a, expert_b


Contested unit
A unit where interpreter disagree. Units are ranked by their mean dissimilarity across all expert pairs.
unit_disagreement


Data checks
Problems that are reported but not fixed: missing membership values, target codes that don’t match the XX0.0 pattern, and totals per unit and expert that aren’t 1.
check_*

Workflow for raster outputs (best candidate)

inc/TASVEG-xref-IUCNGET-output-best-90m.R

## The purpose of this script is to create a spatial output from source
## spatial data using cross-referencing information consolidated in
## membership tables.

## Source classification and spatial data (units):
## > TASVEG 5.0 (vegetation communities)
## Target classification (units):
## > IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology (ecosystem functional groups)
## Output format:
## > Raster GeoTiff files with best candidate target unit, membership and
## > number of supporting interpreters

## This script summarises the minimum set of steps to complete four stages
## of the cross-referencing workflow:
## 1) Data preparation
## 2) Data validation
## 3) Synthesis
## 4) Outputs in preferred format

## Recommended usage:
## R --vanilla < scripts/TASVEG-xref-IUCNGET-output-best-90m.R >\
##  docs-src/reproducibility-notes/TASVEG-xref-IUCNGET-output-best-90m-out.txt

## Step O: Setup

### Benchmarking
start_time <- Sys.time()

### Libraries

#### tidyverse libraries
library(dplyr)
library(readr)
library(tidyr)
library(stringr)

#### For loops
library(foreach)

#### Spatial data
library(terra)
library(sf)
library(fasterize)

#### Cross-referencing
library(ecoSynthesis)
library(geco)

### Paths
here::i_am("scripts/TASVEG-xref-IUCNGET-output-best-90m.R")

out_dir <- here::here("outputs", "best-candidate")
if (!dir.exists(out_dir)) {
  dir.create(out_dir, recursive = TRUE)
}

### Custom functions
source(here::here("scripts", "functions.R"))

## Step 1: data preparation

### Lookup table source classification

TASVEG_xy <- read_sf(here::here(
  "gisdata/LIST_TASVEG_50_STATEWIDE/",
  "TASVEG_5_0.shp"
))


TASVEG_LUT <-
  TASVEG_xy |>
  st_drop_geometry() |>
  select(VEG_GROUP, VEGCODE, VEGCODE_D) |>
  arrange(VEG_GROUP, VEGCODE) |>
  unique() |>
  as_tibble()

not_eligible <- c("OAQ", "OSM", "ORO")
TASVEG <- TASVEG_LUT |>
  mutate(eligible = !(VEGCODE %in% not_eligible)) |>
  lookup_tbl("VEGCODE", "VEGCODE_D", "eligible")

### Lookup table target classification
IUCN_GET <- lookup_tbl(IUCN_GET_LUT, "efg_id", "efg_name")


### Membership tables

memb_data <- foreach(j = dir(here::here("xrefdata")), .combine = bind_rows) %do%
  {
    metadata <- read_csv(
      here::here("xrefdata", j),
      col_names = c("name", "value"),
      n_max = 11,
      show_col_types = F
    )[, 1:2]
    data <- read_csv(here::here("xrefdata", j), skip = 12, show_col_types = F)

    cat(sprintf(
      "Read %s, interpreter %s\n%s\n",
      j,
      metadata[1, 2],
      metadata[11, 2]
    ))

    if ("EFG_1" %in% colnames(data)) {
      pivot_wide_membership_table(
        xref = data,
        original_names = "VEGCODE",
        target_names = sprintf("EFG_%s", 1:4),
        membership_values = sprintf("memb_%s", 1:4),
        expert_name = metadata[[1, 2]],
        round = if_else(grepl("First", metadata[11, 2]), 1, 2)
      )
    } else {
      pivot_membership_matrix(
        xref = data,
        original_names = "VEGCODE",
        target_names = colnames(data)[-1],
        expert_name = metadata[[1, 2]],
        round = if_else(grepl("First", metadata[11, 2]), 1, 2)
      )
    }
  }

memb_data <- memb_data |>
  mutate(round = if_else(expert == "Anne Kitchener", 2, round))

TASVEG_xref <- memb_data |>
  filter(
    !is.na(memb),
    memb > 0
  )

## Step 2: data validation

TASVEG_memb <- read_membership_tbl(
  TASVEG_xref,
  source_id = "VEGCODE",
  target_id = "EFG",
  membership = "memb",
  interpreter = "expert",
  round = "round"
)

TASVEG_clean <- clean_membership(TASVEG_memb, TASVEG, IUCN_GET)


check_membership(TASVEG_clean, TASVEG, IUCN_GET)


## Step 3: synthesis

TASVEG_best_summary <-
  summarise_membership(TASVEG_clean, keep_all = FALSE, which_round = 2)

## Step 4: outputs

### Standard pixel values for Global Ecosystem Atlas
efg_info <- geco_efg_data() |>
  select(efg_code, efg_name, efg_pixel_value, efg_hex_code, efg_rgb_code) |>
  rename("EFG" = "efg_code")

efg_pixel_values <- efg_info |>
  select(EFG, efg_pixel_value)

### Export tabular lookup and synthesis tables
xref_best_tbl <- TASVEG |>
  as_tibble() |>
  left_join(TASVEG_best_summary, by = "VEGCODE") |>
  left_join(efg_info, by = "EFG") |>
  select(
    VEG_GROUP,
    VEGCODE,
    VEGCODE_D,
    eligible,
    EFG,
    efg_name,
    efg_pixel_value,
    efg_hex_code,
    efg_rgb_code,
    round,
    prop_memb,
    total_memb,
    supporting,
    total_interp
  )

write_csv(
  xref_best_tbl,
  here::here(out_dir, "TASVEG-xref-best-candidate.csv")
)

efg_lookup_tbl <- xref_best_tbl |>
  filter(!is.na(EFG)) |>
  summarise(
    n_tasveg_units = n_distinct(VEGCODE),
    .by = c(efg_pixel_value, EFG, efg_name, efg_hex_code, efg_rgb_code)
  ) |>
  left_join(
    as_tibble(IUCN_GET) |>
      select(efg_id, realm_id, realm_name, biome_id, biome_name),
    by = c("EFG" = "efg_id")
  ) |>
  select(
    efg_pixel_value,
    EFG,
    efg_name,
    realm_id,
    realm_name,
    biome_id,
    biome_name,
    efg_hex_code,
    efg_rgb_code,
    n_tasveg_units
  ) |>
  arrange(efg_pixel_value)

write_csv(
  efg_lookup_tbl,
  here::here(out_dir, "IUCN-GET-pixel-lookup.csv")
)

clr_lines <- efg_lookup_tbl |>
  tidyr::separate(efg_rgb_code, into = c("R", "G", "B"), sep = ",") |>
  transmute(
    line = sprintf(
      "%d %s %s %s 255 %s %s",
      efg_pixel_value,
      R,
      G,
      B,
      EFG,
      efg_name
    )
  ) |>
  pull(line)

writeLines(
  clr_lines,
  here::here(out_dir, "TASVEG-xref-target.clr")
)

### Combined attribute table (vector data)
TASVEG_xy_best <- TASVEG_xy |>
  left_join(
    TASVEG_best_summary,
    by = "VEGCODE",
    relationship = "many-to-one"
  ) |>
  left_join(efg_pixel_values, by = "EFG")

### template raster file
rez <- 90
TASVEG_raster <- raster(TASVEG_xy, res = rez)

### Vector to raster using `fasterize`

#### Best candidate

target_raster <- fasterize(
  TASVEG_xy_best,
  TASVEG_raster,
  field = "efg_pixel_value",
  fun = "first"
) |>
  rast()

ctab <- geco_efg_data() |>
  transmute(value = efg_pixel_value, color = efg_hex_code)
coltab(target_raster) <- ctab
out_file <- here::here(out_dir, "TASVEG-xref-target.tiff")

rast_metadata <- c(
  PROJECT = "Ecosystem Indicators Workflows",
  TITLE = "Best candidate ecosystem function group",
  DESCRIPTION = "Synthesis of crossreference from TASVEG 5.0 to IUCN GET"
)
metags(target_raster) <- rast_metadata

writeRaster(target_raster, out_file, overwrite = TRUE)

#### Best candidate membership

memb_raster <- fasterize(
  TASVEG_xy_best,
  TASVEG_raster,
  field = "prop_memb",
  fun = "max"
) |>
  rast()
out_file <- here::here(out_dir, "TASVEG-xref-membership.tiff")

rast_metadata[
  "TITLE"
] <- "Membership for the best candidate ecosystem function group"

metags(memb_raster) <- rast_metadata

writeRaster(memb_raster, out_file, overwrite = TRUE)

#### Supporting interpreters

supp_raster <- fasterize(
  TASVEG_xy_best,
  TASVEG_raster,
  field = "supporting",
  fun = "max"
) |>
  rast()

out_file <- here::here(out_dir, "TASVEG-xref-supporting.tiff")

rast_metadata["TITLE"] <- "Nr. of interpreters supporting assignment"

metags(supp_raster) <- rast_metadata

writeRaster(supp_raster, out_file, overwrite = TRUE)


## Step X: Benchmarking and session info

end_time <- Sys.time()
end_time - start_time

sessionInfo()

## 1. Overview & Methodology

This dataset provides a **`r res_xy[1]` m resolution spatial synthesis** and **tabular cross-reference lookup tables** aligning Tasmania's statewide vegetation map (**TASVEG 5.0**) with Level 3 **Ecosystem Functional Groups (EFGs)** of the **IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology (IUCN GET)**.

### Cross-Referencing & Expert Elicitation Workflow

Following the IUCN standards and guidelines for cross-referencing ecosystem classifications and maps (IUCN, 2025), the workflow proceeded through four stages:

1. **Conceptual Alignment & Eligibility Assessment:**
   - **Source classification:** TASVEG 5.0 (`LIST_TASVEG_50_STATEWIDE`, released November 2025; Kitchener & Harris, 2013), comprising **`r n_total_units` unique mapping units (`VEGCODE`)** in the statewide polygon shapefile across mainland Tasmania and surrounding islands.
   - **Eligibility:** **`r n_eligible_units` mapping units** represent ecological vegetation communities or anthropogenic/modified ecosystems eligible for cross-referencing to the IUCN GET. **`r n_ineligible` mapping units** in the group *Other natural environments* (`r ineligible_list`) represent broad mapping complexes combining multiple distinct ecosystem types or non-vegetated substrates that cannot be unambiguously aligned to a single ecosystem concept without auxiliary spatial data; these `r n_ineligible` units are flagged as `eligible = FALSE` and assigned `NoData` (`NA`) in the spatial rasters. *(Note: Three additional codes present in the TASVEG 5.0 Fire Attributes DBF lookup table—`FPL`, `HUE`, and `SLW`—do not occur as polygons in the statewide shapefile).*
   - **Target classification:** IUCN Global Ecosystem Typology (Keith et al., 2022) at **Level 3: Ecosystem Functional Groups (EFGs)**.

2. **Two-Round Structured Expert Elicitation:**
   - `r n_interp` domain experts (MGT, DAK, AL, AK, JB) independently assessed the fuzzy membership ($0 < \text{memb} \le 1$, summing to $1.0$ per source unit and interpreter) of each eligible TASVEG 5.0 community across candidate IUCN GET EFGs.
   - Discrepancies and contested units from **Round 1** were systematically reviewed in group discussions, after which experts provided revised assessments in **Round `r round_nr`**.

3. **Synthesis ("Best Candidate" / Winner-Takes-All):**
   - Using the validated **Round `r round_nr`** assessments across all **`r n_interp` interpreters**, membership scores were aggregated by `VEGCODE` using `ecoSynthesis::summarise_membership(..., keep_all = FALSE, which_round = 2)`.
   - For each source `VEGCODE`, the candidate EFG receiving the highest **proportion of total membership votes (`prop_memb`)** across the `r n_interp` interpreters was selected as the **best candidate**.
   - Across the `r n_eligible_units` eligible TASVEG 5.0 units, **`r n_efgs` IUCN GET Ecosystem Functional Groups** were selected as best candidates, with `prop_memb` ranging from **`r sprintf("%.2f", prop_min)` to `r sprintf("%.2f", prop_max)`** (median **`r sprintf("%.2f", prop_median)`**, mean **`r sprintf("%.3f", prop_mean)`**). For **`r supp_max_row$n_units` of `r n_eligible_units` units** (`r sprintf("%.1f%%", supp_max_row$pct_area)` of mapped area), all `r supp_max_row$supporting` interpreters assigned non-zero membership to the winning EFG (`supporting = ` `r supp_max_row$supporting`).

4. **Spatial Rasterization (`r res_xy[1]` m GeoTIFFs):**
   - The synthesised table was joined to the TASVEG 5.0 polygon geometries (`TASVEG_5_0.shp`) and rasterized at **`r res_xy[1]` m × `r res_xy[2]` m resolution** in ``r crs_label`` using `fasterize::fasterize()`.
   - Standard integer pixel codes (`efg_pixel_value`) and official hex color tables (`efg_hex_code`) from the Global Ecosystems Atlas (`geco` R package) were embedded into the target GeoTIFF.

---

## 2. File Inventory

| File Name | Format | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `TASVEG-xref-target.tiff` | GeoTIFF (`r datatype(r_target)` / integer, embedded color table) | **Best-candidate IUCN GET Ecosystem Functional Group** at `r res_xy[1]` m resolution. Pixel values (``r min(efg_lut$efg_pixel_value)`` to ``r max(efg_lut$efg_pixel_value)``) correspond to `efg_pixel_value` in `IUCN-GET-pixel-lookup.csv`. |
| `TASVEG-xref-membership.tiff` | GeoTIFF (`r datatype(r_memb)` / float32) | **Proportion of total membership votes (`prop_memb`)** supporting the best-candidate EFG in Round `r round_nr` (continuous values from ``r sprintf("%.2f", memb_minmax[1])`` to ``r sprintf("%.2f", memb_minmax[2])``). Quantifies thematic/cross-referencing certainty. |
| `TASVEG-xref-supporting.tiff` | GeoTIFF (`r datatype(r_supp)` / integer) | **Number of supporting interpreters (`supporting`)** out of `r n_interp` who assigned $>0$ membership to the best-candidate EFG in Round `r round_nr` (integer values: `r paste(sprintf("\x60%d\x60", sort(freq_supp$value)), collapse = ", ")`). |
| `TASVEG-xref-best-candidate.csv` | CSV (UTF-8, `r nrow(xref_tbl)` rows) | **Complete TASVEG 5.0 to IUCN GET synthesis table** linking all `r n_total_units` statewide shapefile `VEGCODE` units (``r n_eligible_units`` eligible + ``r n_ineligible`` non-eligible) to their best-candidate EFG, pixel value, color codes, `prop_memb`, and `supporting` counts. |
| `IUCN-GET-pixel-lookup.csv` | CSV (UTF-8, `r nrow(efg_lut)` rows) | **Raster pixel value dictionary** mapping the `r nrow(efg_lut)` integer codes (`efg_pixel_value`: ``r min(efg_lut$efg_pixel_value)``–``r max(efg_lut$efg_pixel_value)``) in `TASVEG-xref-target.tiff` to EFG codes, EFG names, IUCN GET Realm/Biome hierarchy, RGB/Hex colors, and number of TASVEG communities. |
| `TASVEG-xref-target.qml` | QGIS Style XML | **QGIS layer style file** for `TASVEG-xref-target.tiff`. Place in the same folder as the `.tiff` to automatically display official Global Ecosystems Atlas colors and EFG code + name labels in QGIS. |
| `TASVEG-xref-target.clr` | GDAL / ESRI Color Map | **Standard RGBA color map file** (`value R G B A label`) for styling `TASVEG-xref-target.tiff` in ArcGIS, GDAL, or other GIS software. |
| `datapackage.json` | JSON (Frictionless Data) | **Machine-readable Frictionless Data Package specification** describing all tabular schemas, field definitions, and spatial raster metadata. |
| `.zenodo.json` | JSON | **Zenodo deposit metadata** (creators, ORCIDs, affiliations, license, keywords, and related DOIs/URLs). |
| `LICENSE` | Plain text / Markdown | **Full licensing terms** (CC BY 4.0 for data/docs, CC BY 3.0 AU attribution for TASVEG 5.0, MIT for code). |
| `README.md` / `README.qmd` | Markdown / Quarto | **Dataset documentation file** and the reproducible Quarto template that generates it. |

## 3. Spatial Specifications

All three GeoTIFF files (`TASVEG-xref-target.tiff`, `TASVEG-xref-membership.tiff`, `TASVEG-xref-supporting.tiff`) share an identical spatial grid:

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **Coordinate Reference System (CRS)** | ``r crs_label`` |
| **Spatial Resolution** | ``r sprintf("%g m × %g m", res_xy[1], res_xy[2])`` (``r sprintf("%.4f km²", pixel_km2)`` / ``r sprintf("%.2f ha", pixel_ha)`` per pixel) |
| **Grid Dimensions** | ``r sprintf("%d rows × %d columns × %d band", n_rows, n_cols, n_bands)`` (``r format(total_cells, big.mark = ",")`` total grid cells) |
| **Mapped Onshore Pixels** | ``r format(mapped_pixels, big.mark = ",")`` valid pixels (``r sprintf("%s km²", format(round(mapped_area_km2, 2), big.mark = ",", nsmall = 2))`` total mapped area) |
| **NoData (`NA`) Pixels** | ``r format(nodata_pixels, big.mark = ",")`` pixels (marine/background outside TASVEG polygons + non-eligible units `OAQ`, `ORO`, `OSM`) |
| **Bounding Box (`xmin, xmax, ymin, ymax`)** | ``r sprintf("%.0f, %.0f, %.0f, %.0f", ext_bbox[1], ext_bbox[2], ext_bbox[3], ext_bbox[4])`` (meters, `r paste0(crs_info$authority[1], ":", crs_info$code[1])`) |
| **Rasterization Rule (`fasterize`)** | `TASVEG-xref-target.tiff`: `fun = "first"` on `efg_pixel_value`<br>`TASVEG-xref-membership.tiff`: `fun = "max"` on `prop_memb`<br>`TASVEG-xref-supporting.tiff`: `fun = "max"` on `supporting` |
| **Embedded GDAL Metadata Tags** | `AREA_OR_POINT = Area`<br>`PROJECT = Ecosystem Indicators Workflows`<br>`DESCRIPTION = Synthesis of crossreference from TASVEG 5.0 to IUCN GET`<br>`TITLE = <Layer-specific title>` |

## 4. Lookup Table: Target Pixel Values (`TASVEG-xref-target.tiff`)

The table below lists all **`r n_efgs` IUCN GET Level 3 Ecosystem Functional Groups** present in `TASVEG-xref-target.tiff` (also provided in machine-readable form in `IUCN-GET-pixel-lookup.csv`):

```{r}
#| label: efg-lookup-table
#| results: asis
tbl_rows <- efg_summary_tbl |>
  transmute(
    `Pixel Value (\`efg_pixel_value\`)` = sprintf("**%d**", efg_pixel_value),
    `EFG Code` = sprintf("`%s`", EFG),
    `Ecosystem Functional Group Name (\`efg_name\`)` = efg_name,
    `Realm (\`realm_id\`)` = sprintf("`%s` (%s)", realm_id, realm_name),
    `Biome (\`biome_id\`)` = sprintf("`%s`", biome_id),
    `Hex Color (\`efg_hex_code\`)` = sprintf("`%s`", efg_hex_code),
    `TASVEG Units (\`n_tasveg_units\`)` = as.character(n_tasveg_units),
    `Mapped Pixels (90 m)` = format(count, big.mark = ","),
    `Mapped Area (km²)` = format(round(area_km2, 2), big.mark = ",", nsmall = 2)
  )

total_row <- tibble(
  `Pixel Value (\`efg_pixel_value\`)` = "**Total**",
  `EFG Code` = "—",
  `Ecosystem Functional Group Name (\`efg_name\`)` = sprintf("**%d Ecosystem Functional Groups**", n_efgs),
  `Realm (\`realm_id\`)` = sprintf("**%d Realms**", n_realms),
  `Biome (\`biome_id\`)` = sprintf("**%d Biomes**", n_biomes),
  `Hex Color (\`efg_hex_code\`)` = "—",
  `TASVEG Units (\`n_tasveg_units\`)` = sprintf("**%d**", sum(efg_summary_tbl$n_tasveg_units)),
  `Mapped Pixels (90 m)` = sprintf("**%s**", format(mapped_pixels, big.mark = ",")),
  `Mapped Area (km²)` = sprintf("**%s**", format(round(mapped_area_km2, 2), big.mark = ",", nsmall = 2))
)

kable(
  bind_rows(tbl_rows, total_row),
  format = "pipe",
  align = c("r", "l", "l", "l", "l", "l", "r", "r", "r")
)
```

### Summary of Uncertainty Layers

- **`TASVEG-xref-membership.tiff` (`prop_memb`)**:
  - Represents the proportion of total membership votes across all `r n_interp` interpreters in Round `r round_nr` assigned to the winning EFG:
    $$\text{prop\_memb}_{s, t^*} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{`r n_interp`} m_{s, t^*, i}}{\sum_{t} \sum_{i=1}^{`r n_interp`} m_{s, t, i}}$$
  - Values range from **`r sprintf("%.2f", memb_minmax[1])`** (contested/broadly split source unit) to **`r sprintf("%.2f", memb_minmax[2])`** (unanimous 100% assignment by all `r n_interp` interpreters).
- **`TASVEG-xref-supporting.tiff` (`supporting`)**:
  - Count of interpreters (out of `r n_interp` in Round `r round_nr`) who assigned $m_{s, t^*, i} > 0$ to the best-candidate EFG:
```{r}
#| label: supporting-bullets
#| results: asis
for (i in seq_len(nrow(supp_summary))) {
  row <- supp_summary[i, ]
  unit_word <- ifelse(row$n_units == 1, "TASVEG unit", "TASVEG units")
  cat(sprintf(
    "    - `supporting = %d`: **%d %s** (`%s` pixels / `%s km²` / **%.2f%%** of mapped area)\n",
    row$supporting,
    row$n_units,
    unit_word,
    format(row$pixels, big.mark = ","),
    format(round(row$area_km2, 2), big.mark = ",", nsmall = 2),
    row$pct_area
  ))
}
```

## 5. Tabular Data Dictionaries

### `TASVEG-xref-best-candidate.csv` (`r nrow(xref_tbl)` rows × `r ncol(xref_tbl)` columns)

| Column | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `VEG_GROUP` | `string` | Broad TASVEG 5.0 vegetation group name (e.g., `Rainforest and related scrub`, `Dry eucalypt forest and woodland`). |
| `VEGCODE` | `string` | Three-letter TASVEG 5.0 mapping unit code (primary key, e.g., `AAP`, `WDA`). |
| `VEGCODE_D` | `string` | Full name/description of the TASVEG 5.0 community (e.g., `(AAP) Alkaline pans`). |
| `eligible` | `boolean` | `TRUE` for the `r n_eligible_units` cross-referenced vegetation communities; `FALSE` for `OAQ`, `ORO`, and `OSM` (which have `NA` in subsequent columns). |
| `EFG` | `string` | Best-candidate IUCN GET Level 3 Ecosystem Functional Group code (e.g., `TF1.7`, `T2.5`). |
| `efg_name` | `string` | Full name of the best-candidate EFG. |
| `efg_pixel_value` | `integer` | Integer value representing the EFG in `TASVEG-xref-target.tiff` (``r min(efg_lut$efg_pixel_value)`` to ``r max(efg_lut$efg_pixel_value)``). |
| `efg_hex_code` | `string` | Official hexadecimal color code (`#RRGGBB`) from the `geco` package. |
| `efg_rgb_code` | `string` | Comma-separated RGB triplet (`R,G,B`). |
| `round` | `integer` | Expert elicitation round (``r round_nr``). |
| `prop_memb` | `numeric` | Proportion of total Round `r round_nr` membership votes assigned to the best-candidate EFG (``r sprintf("%.2f", prop_min)`` to ``r sprintf("%.2f", prop_max)``). |
| `total_memb` | `numeric` | Total membership weight across all interpreters in Round `r round_nr` (``r n_interp``). |
| `supporting` | `integer` | Number of interpreters in Round `r round_nr` supporting the best-candidate EFG with membership $> 0$ (``r min(xref_elig$supporting)`` to ``r max(xref_elig$supporting)``). |
| `total_interp` | `integer` | Total number of interpreters assessing the unit in Round `r round_nr` (``r n_interp``). |

### `IUCN-GET-pixel-lookup.csv` (`r nrow(efg_lut)` rows × `r ncol(efg_lut)` columns)

| Column | Type | Description |
|---|---|---|
| `efg_pixel_value` | `integer` | Integer pixel code in `TASVEG-xref-target.tiff` (``r min(efg_lut$efg_pixel_value)`` to ``r max(efg_lut$efg_pixel_value)``). |
| `EFG` | `string` | IUCN GET Level 3 code (e.g., `T2.3`). |
| `efg_name` | `string` | Full name of the Ecosystem Functional Group. |
| `realm_id` | `string` | IUCN GET Level 1 Realm code (`r paste(sprintf("\x60%s\x60", unique(efg_lut$realm_id)), collapse = ", ")`). |
| `realm_name` | `string` | IUCN GET Level 1 Realm name. |
| `biome_id` | `string` | IUCN GET Level 2 Functional Biome code (`r paste(sprintf("\x60%s\x60", unique(efg_lut$biome_id)), collapse = ", ")`). |
| `biome_name` | `string` | IUCN GET Level 2 Functional Biome name. |
| `efg_hex_code` | `string` | Hexadecimal color code (`#RRGGBB`). |
| `efg_rgb_code` | `string` | Comma-separated RGB color code (`R,G,B`). |
| `n_tasveg_units` | `integer` | Count of TASVEG 5.0 communities assigned to this EFG as their best candidate. |

## 6. How to Use This Dataset

### In QGIS or ArcGIS
- **QGIS:** Keep `TASVEG-xref-target.qml` in the same folder as `TASVEG-xref-target.tiff`. When you drag and drop `TASVEG-xref-target.tiff` into QGIS, it will automatically apply the official Global Ecosystems Atlas color palette and display both the EFG code and full name in the Layers legend.
- **ArcGIS Pro / GDAL:** Use `TASVEG-xref-target.clr` to import the color map and labels, or join `IUCN-GET-pixel-lookup.csv` on the `Value` = `efg_pixel_value` field.

### In R (`terra`)

```r
library(terra)
library(readr)

# 1. Load the three 90m rasters and lookup table
r_target <- rast("TASVEG-xref-target.tiff")
r_memb   <- rast("TASVEG-xref-membership.tiff")
r_supp   <- rast("TASVEG-xref-supporting.tiff")
lut      <- read_csv("IUCN-GET-pixel-lookup.csv")

# 2. Attach EFG labels as raster factor levels (categorical RAT)
levels(r_target) <- data.frame(
  id = lut$efg_pixel_value,
  EFG = lut$EFG,
  efg_name = lut$efg_name
)

plot(r_target, main = "Best-Candidate IUCN GET Ecosystem Functional Group (90 m)")

# 3. Example: Filter/mask to high-confidence areas (prop_memb >= 0.8 and supporting == 5)
high_conf_mask <- (r_memb >= 0.8) & (r_supp == 5)
r_target_high_conf <- mask(r_target, high_conf_mask, maskvalues = c(0, NA))
```

### In Python (`rasterio` / `pandas`)

```python
import pandas as pd
import rasterio

lut = pd.read_csv("IUCN-GET-pixel-lookup.csv")
xref = pd.read_csv("TASVEG-xref-best-candidate.csv")

with rasterio.open("TASVEG-xref-target.tiff") as src_targ, \
     rasterio.open("TASVEG-xref-membership.tiff") as src_memb:
    efg_arr = src_targ.read(1)
    memb_arr = src_memb.read(1)
    crs = src_targ.crs
    transform = src_targ.transform
```

### Reproducing the Outputs and Documentation from Source

These files are generated by [`inc/TASVEG-xref-IUCNGET-output-best-90m.R`](https://github.com/Ecosystem-Indicators-Workflows/TASVEG-XREF/blob/main/inc/TASVEG-xref-IUCNGET-output-best-90m.R) and [`output-best-candidate/README.qmd`](README.qmd) in the main workflow repository:

```bash
# 1. Download TASVEG 5.0 source shapefile into gisdata/
R --vanilla < scripts/TASVEG-data-download.R > docs-src/reproducibility-notes/TASVEG-data-download-out.txt

# 2. Run the synthesis and 90m GeoTIFF + CSV export
R --vanilla < scripts/TASVEG-xref-IUCNGET-output-best-90m.R > docs-src/reproducibility-notes/TASVEG-xref-IUCNGET-output-best-90m-out.txt

# 3. Re-render README.md with updated statistics from the generated files
quarto render output-best-candidate/README.qmd
```

**Required R packages:** `dplyr`, `readr`, `tidyr`, `stringr`, `foreach`, `terra`, `sf`, `fasterize`, `here`, `knitr`, `jsonlite`, plus GitHub packages `ecoSynthesis` and `Global-Ecosystems-Atlas/geco`.
